transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-02-07 16:00 UTC
Duration: 57 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Riley Torres (Redwood SE), Janelle Kim (Redwood Product), Dana Cole (VectorPath ML), Marcus Liu (VectorPath SRE), Priya Kapoor (VectorPath Head ML), Owen Park (VectorPath Infra)

Summary (auto): quick recap at top — customer saw a 2-6% accuracy drop after quantizing to AWQ+INT8 combination on their 13B model. Focus: reproduce, bisect, propose runtime fallbacks for on-prem.

Topics: quantization paths (GPTQ vs AWQ), FP8 feasibility for onprem, KV cache coherence and eviction, batching heuristics, runtime fallbacks and rollbacks, instrumentation for bisect.

00:00:15 Samir: Hey everyone, thanks for carving time. we got the notes from Dana and some of the failing prompts, right?
00:00:22 Dana: Yep, sent last night, maybe 1,500 examples, mostly chat prompts, some long context ones. hope that worked — sorry if formatting was weird.
00:00:30 Riley: Got it. quick meta: our goal is first to reproduce locally on your private cluster, then run a layerwise bisect if needed, and avoid blanket fallback to FP32 which kills throughput.
00:01:05 Marcus: Quick network note — our cluster is air-gapped but we have a bastion. Owen will provide access. we expect runs to be noisy because other job tenants share NVMe.
00:01:25 Priya: we care about top-line quality on NLU tests and a couple of intent extraction tasks. SLAs: user-facing latency must stay under 200ms p50 for short prompts.
00:01:40 Riley: noted. so two constraints: quality loss (2-6% on our eval) and latency SLO. the quant profile that triggered this was AWQ with last-8 layers in INT8, rest AWQ-3? (audio: speaker overlaps)
00:02:05 Dana: yes, we used the community AWQ export; we then applied an extra pass of per-channel clipping.
00:02:18 Samir: okay. let's walk through what we've instrumented. Riley, you want to lead on traces?
00:02:25 Riley: sure. first observation from their traces: KV cache miss spikes correlated with some of the failing prompts — esp those with long prefixes. it looks like the cache indexing changed after quantization, maybe due to tokenization chunking differences at runtime.
00:03:05 Marcus: hmm, we did change the tokenizer pipeline slightly to force byte-pair normalize, could be related.
00:03:15 Riley: yes, small tokenizer drift can produce different attention patterns, shifting token positions and resulting in different KV reuse — that amplifies quantization error because tokens that previously hit cached key/values now recompute with quantized weights.
00:03:42 Dana: so it's not purely model weights?
00:03:46 Riley: It's an interaction: quantization reduces numeric headroom; combined with different cache behavior you can amplify small numerical differences into observable quality regressions.
00:04:05 Priya: is that an AWQ-specific issue or would GPTQ behave similarly?
00:04:12 Riley: GPTQ tends to give better layerwise preservation for some architectures, but AWQ is more aggressive and faster. GPTQ may reduce the regression but costs more disk and slightly higher latency on on‑prem kernels. there's no silver bullet.
00:04:35 Samir: Also FP8 is an option — FP8 (E4M3) with mixed casting on KV matmuls keeps dynamic range, but our onprem runtime needs CUDA+cutlass support; on some older nodes FP8 kernels aren't mature and can regress latency.
00:04:58 Owen: our fleet is a mix of A10G and older A100 gen1; we can provision newer cards but that's a procurement ask.
00:05:10 Riley: right. so our staged proposal: 1) reproduce on your cluster with the same quant artifacts, 2) run layerwise forward-only unquantized traces to find layers with largest contribution to loss (layerwise bisect), 3) evaluate targeted dequant (keep critical layers in FP16/FP32), 4) if still bad, consider rolling runtime fallback (per-request) to a slower but correct model shard.
00:05:45 Marcus: per-request fallback — that sounds complex for onprem given SLOs. how would that route be signalled?
00:05:52 Janelle: we can implement a lightweight runtime shim: inference router checks a per-prompt quality heuristic (logprob delta on a small prefix) and if it appears risky, route to FP16 path that has a separate slower replica. that avoids whole-cluster degradation.
00:06:20 Dana: interesting. can we also do a canary that flags prompts for review?
00:06:24 Samir: yes — we have instrumentation that computes cand-perplexity delta and surface examples to your SRE/ML team.
00:06:34 00:06:34 Marcus: audio glitch there — sorry.
00:06:40 Riley: moving on — batching interplay: we saw batches of 8 had slightly better throughput but some prompts with long context become OOM when we try to raise batch size, so cache eviction policy matters. the runtime currently evicts LRU segments per micro-batch, but the eviction epoch could be tuned to preserve long prefix KV for chatty flows.
00:07:12 Dana: can you explain eviction epoch?
00:07:15 Riley: sure — think of KV cache segments sharded and we evict by segment age; if you extend segment retention for high-reuse flows you keep more KV but memory pressure rises. one hack is adaptive retention: tag flows that are chatty and boost retention.
00:07:38 Priya: that's promising if we can detect chatty sessions cheaply.
00:07:42 Riley: token-level heuristics or conversation-id sticky policy works. cheap and often good enough.
00:07:50 Samir: next, kernel-level noise: quantized GEMM kernels show slightly different rounding behavior that surfaces in top-k probabilities. Riley turned on StridedTrace and saw layer 22 and 23 had most variance.
00:08:12 Riley: right. layer 22's attention qkv matmul shows higher variance in fp32 vs int8 simulation; layer 23 is the first feed-forward with gating and quantized activation lookup; combined they amplify errors.
00:08:30 Dana: can we just keep layers 22-24 in fp16?
00:08:33 Riley: yes that's the simplest targeted fix — keep the offending layers in fp16. but you must benchmark latency/throughput impact; often it's small because those layers are compute-light relative to the whole forward.
00:08:46 Marcus: what about memory/disk overhead for storing mixed-precision checkpoints in onprem?
00:08:51 Riley: negligible — we store a separate small metadata map that says which layer is stored in what precision; actual checkpoint size may increase ~4-6% depending on layers left in fp32.
00:09:05 Samir: now about AWQ vs GPTQ: AWQ is faster to quantize and has smaller artifact size but less deterministic layerwise-preservation; GPTQ gives better per-layer MSE property but can produce larger disk and slightly slower forward due to dequantization steps.
00:09:27 Dana: is there a hybrid approach? e.g., AWQ baseline + GPTQ on suspect layers?
00:09:33 Riley: exactly — we recommend hybrid quantization: run AWQ globally and then GPTQ on the top-k sensitive layers identified by bisect. This gets you AWQ speed and GPTQ accuracy where it matters.
00:09:49 Priya: what's the recommended automated bisect cadence? nightly?
00:09:53 Samir: depends on release cadence — for a large rollout, run a full bisect in staging per candidate model, and nightly smoke tests for regressions in prod. we can shard bisect and parallelize pairs.
00:10:10 00:10:10 Owen: question about orchestration — our private control plane can't call Redwood endpoints. can we run the bisect agent entirely offline?
00:10:18 Samir: yes, we have a self-contained bench agent (redwood-bench-agent) that runs in air-gapped mode, writes results to an encrypted bundle you upload. we only need outbound for telemetry optionality; for this work we'll stay offline.
00:10:34 Marcus: good. please share the agent binary and run instructions.
00:10:38 Samir: will do. link in notes.
00:10:42 Riley: perf telemetry we need: per-layer activations, top-k probability deltas, kernel timings (ms), KV hit/miss rates, and batch contention stats. we'll supply a config for trace level and expected overhead.
00:11:04 Dana: what overhead are we talking?
00:11:07 Riley: low-medium depending on sampling — full trace adds ~10-20% wall time; sampled traces ~2-4%. for bisect runs you're okay with full trace.
00:11:18 Samir: let's talk about rollout safety: we propose three fences — canary, metric thresholds, and automatic rollback.
00:11:26 Janelle: Canary: 1% traffic to quantized fleet for 48h. Metric thresholds: rollout stops if eval set accuracy drops >1.5% or if latency p95 increases >20%. Automatic rollback: control-plane triggers a config switch and routes back to FP16 pool.
00:11:45 Marcus: how quick is rollout rollback on onprem?
00:11:48 Riley: depends on instance provisioning. if you have a warm FP16 pool, rollback is near-instant (~minutes). cold provisioning can be tens of minutes. recommend maintaining a small warm pool for critical services.
00:12:02 Dana: warm pool cost?
00:12:04 Samir: it's similar to reserved capacity pricing; we can share cost models — Janelle will send a model.
00:12:12 Priya: let's get more concrete with the bisect plan.
00:12:16 Riley: plan: step 1) baseline reproduce using their exact artifact (AWQ+clip) and provided prompt set. step 2) run per-layer swap: for N layers we run N+1 runs where each run dequantizes a single layer (fp16) to see delta. step 3) accumulate deltas, sort layers by impact; step 4) create hybrid artifact (AWQ globally + GPTQ on top K layers or keep top K layers in fp16).
00:12:48 Dana: how long will N runs take?
00:12:52 Riley: for a 40-layer 13B model at single GPU throughput we can parallelize across GPUs; expect ~6-12 hours if parallelized, or 24-36 hours serial. we'll give an estimate based on your fleet size.
00:13:08 Marcus: we have 6 GPUs for this test set.
00:13:11 Riley: then plan on about 8-10 hours with parallelization.
00:13:15 Samir: instrumentation will also capture kernel-level noise; if we see nondeterministic variance we may need to pin CUDA/CuBLAS versions or use deterministic kernels.
00:13:28 Owen: we can pin kernel versions but might impact other workloads.
00:13:31 Dana: earlier you mentioned model shims. how invasive are runtime fallbacks? do we need code changes to our inference service?
00:13:40 Riley: minimal: the router needs to be capable of routing based on a quality check or a header flag. Redwood's agent exposes a small library to evaluate candidate delta cheaply — it's a fast forward for first 8 tokens and compute a logprob delta. it's a default drop-in with ~3-4 API calls.
00:13:57 Marcus: that sounds fine. security-wise, agent runs locally so no data leaves the cluster.
00:14:02 Samir: next, discuss AWQ tuning knobs: per-channel vs per-tensor scaling, clip thresholds, and per-group granularity. small changes to clip can shift accuracy by a percent point.
00:14:20 Dana: do you have heuristics for clip thresholds?
00:14:23 Riley: we start with median absolute deviation heuristics and then grid-search with holdout. AWQ hyper is sensitive; a two-step approach (global then per-layer refine) works best. we'll supply a param sweep config.
00:14:40 Priya: what about mixed INT8+FP8 experiments — any wins?
00:14:45 Riley: mixed FP8 for attention + INT8 for linear projections has shown promise — FP8 keeps dynamic range in attention softmax inputs, INT8 covers dense matmuls. but FP8 kernels need hardware/driver support and careful calibration.
00:15:03 Samir: for onprem, we often recommend trying INT8+FP16 targeted layers first, then try FP8 if hardware supports it. FP8 can be a tailwind but operational complexity is higher.
00:15:18 Dana: regression pasture: is this more likely model-inherent or a pipeline issue?
00:15:22 Riley: likely both. tokenization drift + aggressive AWQ settings + KV cache changes = emergent regressions. that's why bisect is useful to decouple these.
00:15:34 00:15:34 Marcus: quick aside — do we have a guardrail to detect tokenization drift before quant?
00:15:40 Janelle: yes, we recommend a pre-flight tokenizer checksum and sample pass that ensures identical token counts on canonical inputs; we can include that in the bench agent.
00:15:52 Dana: nice.
00:15:55 Samir: operational checklist for the run: agent binary, prompt corpus, holdout set, environment spec (CUDA, driver, kernel), trace config. Marcus to open bastion. Dana to upload corpus. Samir to upload run configs and the hybrid workflow script.
00:16:18 Riley: potential pitfalls: nondeterministic math on older drivers, batch scheduling jitter, and NVMe swap causing sporadic latency — we'll log I/O stats too.
00:16:33 Priya: if bisect identifies sensitive layers but hybrid quant still fails, what are options?
00:16:39 Riley: options: 1) keep more layers in fp16, 2) use GPTQ on more layers and accept slightly higher forward cost, 3) degrade per-request fidelity heuristics (shorten context) for failing flows, or 4) invest in newer HW with FP8 support.
00:17:02 Dana: I like the per-request shortening idea as a mitigation — degrade gracefully.
00:17:06 Samir: yes, it's often acceptable for chatty sessions to truncate older context if the model preserves core state.
00:17:13 Owen: any recommended experimentation order?
00:17:16 Riley: reproduce -> layerwise bisect -> targeted dequant -> hybrid GPTQ on top K -> runtime fallback/canonicalization -> consider HW or FP8.
00:17:28 Marcus: schedule wise, after this call we'll await the corpus and agent access — then Redwood runs reproduce and returns a baseline report.
00:17:37 Dana: question: are there reproducible seed knobs? our devs saw slightly different delta when running repeated runs.
00:17:44 Riley: yes, set cudnn deterministic flags and seed RNGs, but be aware it can slow kernels. for bisect you want determinism even if slower. we'll provide recommended flags.
00:17:59 Samir: sudo recap now?
00:18:02 Samir: Recap: reproduce on your cluster (Samir/Riley run), run layerwise bisect, produce layer-sensitivity ranking, propose hybrid artifact and test throughput/latency impact, implement lightweight runtime fallback for risky prompts, and recommend warm FP16 pool for fast rollback.
00:18:24 Janelle: plus deliverables: runbook, agent binary, param sweep configs, and cost/latency model.
00:18:32 Dana: sounds good.
00:18:35 Samir: any final Qs?
00:18:38 Priya: timeline ok: we'll aim to have tokens and access by Monday, Feb 9.
00:18:44 Marcus: I'll open the bastion and send keys today.
00:18:47 Owen: I'll check driver consistency and list GPU SKUs.
00:18:51 Samir: perfect. thanks everyone. we'll target the benchmark by Feb 14 and a follow-up sync for results week of Feb 16.
00:18:59 00:18:59 (meeting quiet, some side chatter)
00:19:20 Speaker 5: [inaudible]
00:20:45 Samir: small note — we'll attach a short table in the report: candidate profiles (AWQ-global, AWQ+GPTQ-topK, Full-GPTQ, FP8-mixed) and expected perf delta and disk size.
00:21:12 Riley: final technical nit: quant noise also can interact with attention scaling; if you see systematic bias in logits we may need to recalibrate layernorm/gains.
00:21:35 Dana: okay noted, love the thoroughness.
00:21:40 Samir: thanks — meeting ended at 16:57 UTC.
